subtopics.title: Alimentary canal and associated glands
subtopics.theory_md:
**Canal:** mouth -> pharynx -> oesophagus -> stomach (cardiac, fundus, body, pyloric) -> small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum) -> large intestine (caecum with appendix, colon, rectum) -> anus. Food moves by **peristalsis**.

**Glands:** salivary (parotid, submandibular, sublingual); gastric glands; **liver** (largest gland, makes bile, stored in gall bladder); **pancreas** (exocrine juice plus insulin and glucagon); intestinal glands. Bile and pancreatic juice enter the duodenum through the common bile duct (sphincter of Oddi).

Wall layers, outside in: serosa, muscularis, submucosa, mucosa.
subtopics.basics_md: Digestion is a one-way tube. Glands pour juices into it at fixed points, like feeder pipes joining a main line.
key_points: Order of the canal from mouth to anus
Three pairs of salivary glands; liver, gall bladder and pancreas open into the duodenum
Liver is the largest gland; bile is stored in the gall bladder
Stomach parts: cardiac, fundus, body, pyloric
Wall layers: serosa, muscularis, submucosa, mucosa

subtopics.title: Disorders of the digestive and respiratory systems
subtopics.theory_md:
**Digestive:** **jaundice** (bilirubin builds up, yellow skin and eyes; liver or bile duct); **peptic ulcer** (*H. pylori*, excess acid); **diarrhoea** (frequent watery stools); **constipation**; **indigestion**; **gallstones**; **hepatitis**.

**Respiratory:** **asthma** (allergic narrowing of bronchioles, wheezing); **bronchitis** (inflamed bronchi, cough); **emphysema** (alveolar walls damaged, smoking, less surface area); **pneumonia** (alveoli fill with fluid, bacteria *Streptococcus pneumoniae*); **tuberculosis** (*Mycobacterium tuberculosis*); **occupational** (silicosis, asbestosis).
subtopics.basics_md: Each disease is just something going wrong in one organ: a blocked pipe, an infected lining, or a damaged exchange surface.

subtopics.title: Digestive system as a process plant
subtopics.theory_md:
Engineering reading of the canal (the answer for both mid 2025 questions):
- **Mouth:** teeth = crusher (size reduction, more surface area); saliva = first catalytic reactor.
- **Oesophagus:** peristalsis = conveyor/peristaltic pump.
- **Stomach:** stirred acid batch reactor; HCl pH 1.5-2 with pepsin; mucus lining = corrosion protection; pyloric sphincter = valve.
- **Small intestine:** bicarbonate neutralisation, enzymes, then **villi** = large-area mass-transfer unit.
- **Large intestine:** dewatering, by-product recovery (water, vitamin K).
- **Anus:** waste discharge valve (sphincters).
subtopics.basics_md: A food factory: crush, mix with acid, neutralise, extract the useful stuff, dry the waste, discharge.
key_points: Teeth = size reduction; stomach = acidic stirred reactor
Peristalsis = peristaltic pump/conveyor; sphincters = valves
Villi give large surface area for mass transfer
Enzymes = catalysts, bile = emulsifier
Large intestine = water recovery; anus = waste discharge

questions.q: Which part of the digestive system acts as a peristaltic pump and which as a reactor? Justify.
questions.model_answer_md:
1. **Oesophagus (and intestine) = peristaltic pump:** waves of muscle contraction push the bolus forward, even against gravity, without moving parts touching the food.
2. **Stomach = stirred acid batch reactor:** churning mixes food with HCl (pH 1.5-2) and pepsin; the mucus lining protects the wall, like a corrosion-resistant lining.
points: Stomach churning = stirred reactor with acid and enzyme

Stomach: acid batch reactor, mucus as corrosion protection
Small intestine: neutralisation and villi for mass transfer
Large intestine: dewatering and by-product recovery; anus as discharge valve

subtopics.title: Respiratory tract and mechanism of breathing
subtopics.theory_md:
**Pathway:** nostrils -> nasal chamber -> pharynx -> larynx -> **trachea** (C-shaped cartilage rings) -> bronchi -> bronchioles -> **alveoli** (exchange surface). Lungs lie in a double-layered **pleural** sac.

**Inspiration (active):** diaphragm contracts and flattens, external intercostals lift ribs and sternum -> thoracic volume rises -> intrapulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric (Boyle's law, $P\propto 1/V$) -> air flows in.
**Expiration (resting, passive):** muscles relax, volume falls, pressure rises above atmospheric, air flows out. Forced expiration uses internal intercostals and abdominal muscles.
subtopics.basics_md: Air goes wherever pressure is lower. Making the chest bigger lowers the pressure inside, so air rushes in.
key_points: Pathway nostril to alveoli with trachea rings and pleura
Inspiration: diaphragm contracts, ribs lift, volume rises, pressure falls
Air flows from high to low pressure (Boyle's law)
Resting expiration is passive

questions.why: Flattening increases thoracic volume.

questions.why: Volume rise lowers the pressure, so air flows in.

questions.q: Explain how air flows into the lungs during inhalation using pressure gradients.
questions.model_answer_md:
1. Air moves from **higher to lower pressure**.
2. **Diaphragm contracts and flattens**; **external intercostals contract** and lift ribs and sternum.
3. Thoracic and lung **volume increases**.
4. By Boyle's law ($P\propto 1/V$) **intrapulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric**.
5. Air flows in down this gradient until pressures equalise.
points: Flow from high to low pressure
Boyle's law: pressure falls below atmospheric

subtopics.title: Gas exchange, transport and control
subtopics.theory_md:
**Exchange** is by diffusion down partial-pressure gradients across the thin alveolar-capillary membrane: alveolar $pO_2\approx104$ mmHg vs 40 in venous blood; $pCO_2$ 40 vs 45. $CO_2$ is far more soluble, so a smaller gradient suffices.

**Transport:** $O_2$ about 97% as **oxyhaemoglobin**; $CO_2$ about 70% as **bicarbonate** (carbonic anhydrase in RBC), 20-25% carbamino-Hb. **Bohr effect:** higher $pCO_2$, $H^+$ or temperature shifts the dissociation curve **right**, so Hb releases more $O_2$ to tissues.

**Control:** respiratory rhythm centre in the **medulla** (with pneumotaxic centre in pons); chemosensitive area responds to $CO_2$ and $H^+$.
subtopics.basics_md: Gases move from where there is more of them to where there is less. Active tissues have more CO2 and acid, so haemoglobin lets go of oxygen there.
key_points: Diffusion along partial pressure gradient across alveolar membrane
O2 mainly as oxyhaemoglobin; CO2 mainly as bicarbonate
Bohr effect: more pCO2 shifts curve right, more O2 released
Rate of breathing controlled by medulla; pons only moderates

points: Respiratory rhythm centre sets the rate; pons only moderates it

subtopics.title: Kidney and nephron structure
subtopics.theory_md:
Humans are **ureotelic**: urea is made in the liver and excreted by the kidneys. Path: kidney -> ureter -> urinary bladder -> urethra. Kidney has outer **cortex** and inner **medulla**; each has about **one million nephrons**, the **functional unit**.

**Nephron:** glomerulus (capillary tuft; wide **afferent**, narrow **efferent** arteriole) inside **Bowman's capsule** (together the renal corpuscle) -> **PCT** -> **loop of Henle** (descending, ascending) -> **DCT** -> **collecting duct**. Peritubular capillaries and **vasa recta** surround the tubule.
subtopics.basics_md: A nephron is a tiny filter attached to a long tube. Blood is squeezed through the filter, then the tube takes back what the body still needs.
key_points: Nephron is the structural and functional unit
Renal corpuscle = glomerulus + Bowman's capsule
Order: PCT, loop of Henle, DCT, collecting duct
Afferent arteriole wider than efferent

Glomerulus and Bowman's capsule are only parts of it (renal corpuscle)

subtopics.title: Urine formation and numericals
subtopics.theory_md:
1. **Ultrafiltration** in the glomerulus: blood pressure forces plasma minus proteins into Bowman's capsule. **GFR = 125 mL/min = 180 L/day**.
2. **Selective reabsorption:** about 99% of filtrate returns to blood; PCT takes glucose, amino acids, $Na^+$ and most water. Descending limb permeable to **water**, ascending limb to **salts**.
3. **Tubular secretion:** $H^+$, $K^+$, ammonia added to filtrate.

Net filtration pressure $=P_{GC}-(P_{BC}+\pi_{GC}) = 55-(15+30)=10$ mmHg. Urine about 1.5 L/day.
subtopics.basics_md: Filter everything small, take back what is useful, add a bit more waste to the tube, and what is left is urine.
key_points: Three steps: filtration, reabsorption, secretion
GFR 125 mL/min, 180 L/day
Proteins are not filtered
NFP = glomerular pressure - (capsular pressure + oncotic pressure)
About 99% reabsorbed

questions.q: If GFR is 125 mL/min and 1.5 L of urine is passed per day, find the daily filtrate and the percentage reabsorbed.
questions.model_answer_md:
Filtrate $=125\times1440 = 180000\ \text{mL} = 180\ \text{L/day}$.
Reabsorbed $=180-1.5 = 178.5\ \text{L}$.
$\%\ \text{reabsorbed} = 178.5/180\times100 \approx 99.2\%$.

questions.q: Glomerular capillary pressure is 55 mmHg, capsular pressure 15 mmHg, plasma oncotic pressure 30 mmHg. Find the net filtration pressure.
questions.model_answer_md: $NFP = P_{GC} - (P_{BC} + \pi_{GC}) = 55 - (15+30) = 10\ \text{mmHg}$ (positive, so filtration occurs).

subtopics.title: Kidney as a filter and homeostasis
subtopics.theory_md:
| Water treatment plant | Kidney |
|---|---|
| Intake of raw water | renal artery -> afferent arteriole |
| Screening/filter bed | glomerulus (blocks cells, proteins) |
| Recovery of useful water | PCT, loop of Henle reabsorption |
| Chemical dosing/adjustment | tubular secretion of $H^+$, $K^+$ |
| Concentration control | counter-current system (300 to 1200 mOsm/L) |
| Waste discharge | ureter, bladder |

**Balance:** **ADH** (posterior pituitary) raises water reabsorption; **aldosterone** (adrenal cortex) raises $Na^+$ reabsorption; renin-angiotensin system corrects low GFR; secretion of $H^+$ keeps pH. About 180 L filtered, 1.5 L excreted.
subtopics.basics_md: The kidney is a self-adjusting filter plant: it cleans a large volume, returns almost all of it, and tunes what stays.
key_points: Glomerulus = filter; tubule = recovery and adjustment
Reabsorption of about 99% of filtrate
Controls water (ADH), Na+ (aldosterone), pH (H+ secretion)
Counter-current mechanism concentrates urine

About 180 L filtered per day, 99% returned, about 1.5 L urine
Balance: water by ADH, Na+ by aldosterone, pH by H+ secretion, osmolarity by counter-current

questions.q: Why does a dialysis machine resemble the nephron?

It copies the glomerular filtration and counter-current exchange of the nephron.

subtopics.title: Bones of the skeleton
subtopics.theory_md:
Adult skeleton: **206 bones** = **axial 80** (skull 29, vertebral column 26, sternum 1, ribs 24) + **appendicular 126** (pectoral girdle 4, pelvic girdle 2, limbs 60 each pair).

Vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 1 sacrum, 1 coccyx. Each limb: 30 bones (arm: humerus, radius, ulna, 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges).

**Bone material:** about two-thirds mineral (**calcium phosphate / hydroxyapatite**, stores about 99% of body calcium) and one-third **collagen**. **Osteoblasts** build, **osteoclasts** resorb. Functions: support, protection, movement, red marrow makes blood cells, mineral store.
subtopics.basics_md: Bones are a living scaffold, hard because of calcium minerals and tough because of collagen fibres.

Main mineral in bone is calcium (as calcium phosphate/hydroxyapatite)
Vertebrae 7-12-5-1-1
Osteoblasts form bone, osteoclasts resorb

points: Stored as calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite), about 99% of body calcium

**Joints:** **fibrous** (immovable: skull sutures); **cartilaginous** (slightly movable: between vertebrae); **synovial** (freely movable, with synovial fluid, cartilage, ligaments):
- **Ball and socket**: shoulder, hip (all directions)
- **Hinge**: knee, elbow (one plane)

- **Gliding**: carpals

Muscles pull on bones as **levers**; joint = fulcrum.

subtopics.title: Skeleton as an engineered structure
subtopics.theory_md:
**Support:** vertebral column = central column; leg bones = pillars carrying body weight. Bone is a **composite**: collagen resists tension, hydroxyapatite resists compression, like reinforced concrete.
**Protection:** skull = helmet, rib cage = protective cage, vertebrae = conduit for spinal cord.
**Movement:** joints = hinges/pivots, bones = levers. **Wolff's law:** bone remodels to the load it carries.

Stress $\sigma=F/A$; strain $\varepsilon=\Delta L/L$; $E=\sigma/\varepsilon$ (cortical bone about 17 GPa).
subtopics.basics_md: Treat bone like a beam: it carries load, resists bending and adapts when loads change.
key_points: Skeleton is the load-bearing frame, like a steel/RCC frame
Bone is a composite: collagen (tension) plus hydroxyapatite (compression)
Skull and rib cage protect like a helmet and cage
Joints and levers give motion
Wolff's law: bone adapts to load

questions.why: Wolff's law.

points: Support: vertebral column as column, leg bones as pillars carrying load; bone as composite (collagen + hydroxyapatite) like reinforced concrete

questions.q: A femur carries 700 N with a cross-section of 3.5 cm$^2$. Find the stress, and the strain if $E=17$ GPa.
questions.model_answer_md:
$A = 3.5\ \text{cm}^2 = 3.5\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2$
$\sigma = F/A = 700/(3.5\times10^{-4}) = 2.0\times10^{6}\ \text{Pa} = 2.0\ \text{MPa}$
$\varepsilon = \sigma/E = 2.0\times10^{6}/(17\times10^{9}) \approx 1.2\times10^{-4}$ (dimensionless)

subtopics.title: Heart: structure and conduction
subtopics.theory_md:
Four chambers: two thin **atria**, two thick **ventricles** (left wall thickest). Valves: **tricuspid** (right AV), **bicuspid/mitral** (left AV), **semilunar** valves (pulmonary artery, aorta); one-way flow. Heart is **myogenic**.

**Conduction:** **SA node** (pacemaker, right atrium, about 70-75/min) -> atria contract -> **AV node** (delay) -> **bundle of His** -> **Purkinje fibres** -> ventricles contract.

**Double circulation:** pulmonary (right ventricle -> lungs -> left atrium); systemic (left ventricle -> body -> right atrium). Pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood.
subtopics.basics_md: A double pump: the right side sends blood to the lungs, the left side to the whole body.
key_points: Four chambers and valves with positions
SA node is the pacemaker; AV node delays
Path: SA node, AV node, bundle of His, Purkinje fibres
Pulmonary artery deoxygenated, pulmonary vein oxygenated
Left ventricle wall thickest

questions.q: Describe the conducting system of the heart.
questions.model_answer_md:

2. Both atria contract

4. **Bundle of His** and branches carry it down the septum
5. **Purkinje fibres** spread it; ventricles contract from the apex

subtopics.title: Cardiac cycle and cardiac output
subtopics.theory_md:
Cardiac cycle (72 beats/min) lasts **0.8 s**: atrial systole 0.1 s, ventricular systole 0.3 s, joint diastole 0.4 s.
**'Lub'** = AV valves close (start of ventricular systole). **'Dub'** = semilunar valves close (end).

$SV = EDV-ESV$, $\ CO = HR\times SV$, $\ EF = SV/EDV$, $\ T = 60/HR$.
At rest $SV\approx70$ mL, $CO\approx5$ L/min. Normal BP 120/80 mmHg; $MAP\approx DBP+\tfrac13(SBP-DBP)$.
subtopics.basics_md: Each beat ejects a small volume; multiply by beats per minute for flow per minute.
key_points: Cycle 0.8 s at 72/min
Lub = AV closure, dub = semilunar closure
CO = HR x SV
SV = EDV - ESV
BP 120/80 mmHg

questions.q: Heart rate 72 beats/min, stroke volume 70 mL. Find the cardiac output and the duration of one cycle.
questions.model_answer_md:
$CO=HR\times SV=72\times70=5040\ \text{mL/min}\approx5.0\ \text{L/min}$
$T=60/72\approx0.83\ \text{s}$ (about 0.8 s)

questions.q: EDV = 120 mL, ESV = 50 mL, HR = 75/min, SBP 120 and DBP 80 mmHg. Find SV, EF, CO and MAP.
questions.model_answer_md:
$SV=120-50=70\ \text{mL}$
$EF=70/120=58\%$
$CO=75\times70=5250\ \text{mL/min}=5.25\ \text{L/min}$
$MAP=80+\tfrac13(120-80)\approx93\ \text{mmHg}$

subtopics.title: ECG, blood and vessels
subtopics.theory_md:
**Blood:** plasma (55%) + RBC, WBC, platelets. **ECG:** **P** = atrial depolarisation; **QRS** = ventricular depolarisation (start of systole); **T** = ventricular repolarisation.

**Vessels:** arteries (thick elastic wall, high pressure, away from heart), veins (thin wall, **valves**, towards heart), capillaries (one cell thick, exchange). Disorders: hypertension, atherosclerosis, angina, heart failure.
subtopics.basics_md: The ECG is the heart's electrical signature, one wave for each event.
key_points: P wave atrial depolarisation, QRS ventricular depolarisation, T ventricular repolarisation
Arteries thick-walled without valves; veins have valves
Capillaries are the exchange site
Hypertension and atherosclerosis

subtopics.title: Neuron structure
subtopics.theory_md:
**Neuron:** **cell body (soma/cyton)** with nucleus and Nissl's granules; branched **dendrites** receive signals and conduct them **towards** the soma; one long **axon** carries impulses **away**, ending in synaptic knobs. **Myelin sheath** (Schwann cells) insulates the axon, with gaps called **nodes of Ranvier**.

Types: multipolar, bipolar, unipolar. Classification of nerves: **afferent** (sensory) and **efferent** (motor); PNS has somatic and autonomic (sympathetic, parasympathetic) parts.
subtopics.basics_md: A neuron is a wire with branches on the input end and a long insulated cable on the output end.
key_points: Dendrites receive, axon transmits away
Soma contains nucleus and Nissl's granules
Myelin sheath insulates; nodes of Ranvier are gaps
Afferent = sensory, efferent = motor

subtopics.title: Nerve impulse and synapse
subtopics.theory_md:
**Resting potential:** about **-70 mV** inside, kept by the **Na$^+$/K$^+$ pump** (3 Na out, 2 K in). **Stimulus:** Na channels open, Na enters (**depolarisation**, about +30 mV = action potential). Then K channels open, K leaves (**repolarisation**). In myelinated fibres the impulse jumps node to node (**saltatory conduction**, faster).

**Chemical synapse:** impulse at the terminal releases a neurotransmitter (e.g. **acetylcholine**) into the cleft; it binds receptors on the post-synaptic membrane. Nernst: $E=\dfrac{RT}{zF}\ln\dfrac{[\text{out}]}{[\text{in}]}$; $E_K\approx-89$ mV at 37 C.
subtopics.basics_md: A neuron is like a charged battery. The signal is a wave of sodium rushing in and potassium leaving, passed along the membrane.
key_points: Resting potential about -70 mV, maintained by Na/K pump
Depolarisation: Na+ in; repolarisation: K+ out
Saltatory conduction in myelinated fibres
Synapse: neurotransmitter crosses the cleft

questions.why: Na+ rushes in; K+ leaves during repolarisation.

questions.q: Explain how a nerve impulse is generated and conducted.
questions.model_answer_md:
1. Resting potential **-70 mV** (Na/K pump)
2. Stimulus opens Na channels; Na enters: **depolarisation** to +30 mV (action potential)
3. K channels open; K leaves: **repolarisation**
4. Wave spreads along axon; in myelinated fibre it jumps between nodes (saltatory conduction)
5. At the synapse, **acetylcholine** crosses the cleft and excites the next neuron

subtopics.title: Central nervous system and reflex
subtopics.theory_md:
**CNS = brain + spinal cord**, protected by skull, vertebral column, **meninges** (dura, arachnoid, pia) and **cerebrospinal fluid**.

| Part | Function |
|---|---|
| Cerebrum | thinking, memory, voluntary action, sensation |
| Thalamus | relay of sensory signals |
| Hypothalamus | temperature, hunger, hormones |
| Cerebellum | balance and coordination |
| Pons | links parts, moderates breathing |
| Medulla | breathing, heart rate, BP |
| Spinal cord | conduction and reflexes |

**Reflex arc:** receptor -> sensory neuron (dorsal root) -> spinal cord -> motor neuron (ventral root) -> effector.
subtopics.basics_md: The CNS is the control room: sensory data comes in, decisions are made in the brain or cord, commands go out.
key_points: CNS = brain and spinal cord with three meninges and CSF
Cerebrum, cerebellum, medulla roles
Hypothalamus controls temperature and hormones
Reflex arc via spinal cord (dorsal sensory, ventral motor)

Components: cerebrum, thalamus, hypothalamus, cerebellum, pons, medulla, spinal cord with function of each
Integration: sensory input processed in brain/cord, motor output via efferent neurons; reflexes via spinal cord

questions.q: Name the three meninges and the role of CSF.
questions.model_answer_md: **Dura mater** (outer), **arachnoid** (middle), **pia mater** (inner). CSF cushions the brain and cord and carries nutrients and wastes.

subtopics.title: Physiology as engineering: pump, pipe, exchanger
subtopics.theory_md:
- **Heart = pump:** $CO=HR\times SV\approx5$ L/min; valves = check valves.
- **Vessels = pipes:** $\Delta P=QR$ with Poiseuille $R=\dfrac{8\eta L}{\pi r^4}$. Halving the radius raises resistance $2^4=16$ times.
- **Alveolus:** Laplace $P=2\gamma/r$; surfactant lowers $\gamma$ so small alveoli do not collapse. Fick: diffusion $\propto A\,\Delta p/T$ (large area, thin barrier).
- **Bone = beam/column:** $\sigma=F/A$, $E=\sigma/\varepsilon$.
- **Nerve = signalling cable:** myelin raises speed up to about 100 m/s.
subtopics.basics_md: Treat each organ as a device with inputs, outputs and limits, then ordinary mechanics and fluid laws apply.
key_points: Heart as positive-displacement pump with check valves
Resistance goes as 1/r^4 (Poiseuille)
Surfactant reduces surface tension (Laplace)
Lungs maximise area and minimise thickness (Fick)
Bone as a composite load-bearing structure

$R_2/R_1=(1/0.8)^4 = 2.44$.

questions.q: Why do small alveoli not collapse? (Laplace)
questions.model_answer_md: $P=2\gamma/r$: smaller radius needs higher pressure to stay open. **Surfactant** lowers surface tension $\gamma$, so small alveoli stay open.

subtopics.title: Biosensors, electronic tongue and nose
subtopics.theory_md:
**Biosensor:** analytical device with a **biological recognition element** and a **transducer** giving a signal proportional to analyte concentration (e.g. glucometer).
**Components:** bioreceptor (enzyme, antibody, DNA, cell); transducer (electrochemical, optical, thermal, piezoelectric); electronics (amplifier, processor); display.

**Electronic tongue:** array of non-specific chemical sensors for dissolved tastants + pattern recognition (like taste buds + brain). **Electronic nose:** array of gas sensors (metal-oxide, conducting polymer) for volatiles + pattern recognition (like olfactory receptors + brain).
subtopics.basics_md: A biosensor is a detector that pairs something that recognises a chemical with something that turns that recognition into a number.
key_points: Biosensor = bioreceptor + transducer + signal processor
Examples: glucose biosensor
E-tongue: sensor array for liquids; E-nose: sensor array for gases
Both use pattern recognition like the brain

options: Converts the biological response to a measurable signal
questions.why: The bioreceptor recognises; the transducer converts.

points: Definition: biological recognition element plus transducer giving signal proportional to analyte

E-nose: array of gas sensors with pattern recognition, mimics olfactory receptors

subtopics.title: Human eye and camera
subtopics.theory_md:
**Eye parts:** sclera, **cornea**, choroid, **iris** with **pupil**, **lens**, **ciliary muscles**, **retina** (rods for dim light, cones for colour), **fovea**, **optic nerve**, aqueous and vitreous humour.

| Eye | Camera |
|---|---|
| Cornea + lens | Lens |
| Iris/pupil | Aperture/diaphragm |
| Retina | Film/image sensor |
| Ciliary muscles change lens curvature | Focus by moving lens |
| Choroid (dark) | Black inner wall |
| Eyelid | Lens cap/shutter |

Difference: eye lens is flexible (accommodation); camera focuses by moving the lens.
subtopics.basics_md: The eye is a natural camera: lens focuses light on a sensor (the retina), the iris controls how much light gets in.

Retina = image sensor, iris = aperture
